analysis.one_liner: Requires bank bailout repayments to go to paying down the national debt instead of being spent on new programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate committee hearing or vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2008 bailout law, the Treasury could take money banks repaid under TARP and lend it out again for new stabilization programs. This bill would have ended that, requiring every repayment and every dollar from selling government-owned assets to go straight into the Treasury's general fund to reduce the public debt. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, since bailout repayments would pay down the national debt instead of funding new federal lending and intervention programs.

how_it_helps.text: All TARP repayments and proceeds from selling federally acquired assets would be paid into the general fund of the Treasury to reduce the public debt, rather than reused for new bailout or lending programs.

The bill amends the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act so that the pool of money available for re-lending is capped at what was already obligated or spent when the bill passed, ending the revolving use of repaid bailout funds.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury would lose the flexibility to recycle repaid bailout funds into new financial-stability, small-business, or consumer lending programs during the ongoing recovery, and the industries and borrowers those programs supported would lose that funding source.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that the financial crisis was still ongoing in 2009, and requiring repayments to go to debt reduction would have removed the Treasury's ability to redeploy that money quickly if new trouble emerged.

Each dollar paid toward the national debt has only a small immediate effect on most households, while recycled TARP funds supported programs like small-business lending, so the bill trades visible near-term credit support for a diffuse fiscal benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, honestly aimed fiscal-discipline measure: it locks bailout repayments into debt reduction and takes away emergency discretion from the Treasury. That trade is defensible, but the stakes on either side are modest, and the bill offers nothing for the recovery beyond gradual deficit reduction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on June 11, 2009, joined at introduction by Sen. Blanche Lincoln, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The bill would have required all repayments of TARP funds and all proceeds from selling federally acquired assets to be used to reduce the public debt.
No further action was taken after the referral; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and the administration kept the discretion to recycle repaid bailout funds into new stabilization and lending programs, and the industries and borrowers those programs supported kept that funding source.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and industries using recycled funds

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require TARP repayments to go to debt reduction.

for.name: Sen. Blanche Lincoln
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Christopher Dodd (D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Planned to use repaid TARP funds for new programs, including small-business lending, which this bill would have prohibited.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill and a Democratic senator joined at introduction; the six total sponsors split 3 Republicans and 3 Democrats, but the Democratic-led committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Banks and financial institutions receiving or eligible for recycled TARP funds
industries.note: The bill would have cut off the revolving use of repaid bailout money, ending Treasury's ability to route repayments into new lending and support programs for financial firms. Its interest ran against taxpayers' debt reduction.

industries.industry: Small businesses and borrowers in Treasury-backed lending programs
industries.note: Programs funded by recycled TARP repayments, such as small-business lending, would have lost their funding source. Their loss would have been ordinary taxpayers' gain through debt reduction.
